messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-five when he finally walked into the clinic, though his face had the weathered look of someone who had aged a decade in the five years since his daughter drowned. She had been seven years old, and he had been watching her—or he thought he had been watching her—at his brother's beach house on the North Shore. The afternoon had been bright and loud with the noise of children. Marcus, a Samoan man who had built a careful life as a nanny to three families across Brooklyn, had positioned himself on the sand with a book, glancing up at regular intervals. The water that day was deceptively calm, almost glassy, and when he looked again after what he later calculated was perhaps four minutes, Aroha was no longer visible among the wading children. The sound he heard first was not a scream but an absence—the sudden silence of a child not calling out. Then came the chaos: his brother's shouts, the lifeguard running, the terrible smallness of her body when they pulled her from the water. She had aspirated seawater. She was gone before the ambulance arrived.

In the weeks after, Marcus had tried to explain it to people—to his ex-wife, to the families he worked for, to the police who asked their careful questions—but the words would scatter in his mouth. He would begin to describe the moment he realized she was missing, and his voice would simply stop, as though his throat had closed around something too large to pass. He could not finish a sentence about that day without losing the thread entirely, unable to retrieve the sequence of events or even the precise words people had spoken. What remained were fragments: the sound of the lifeguard's whistle, the specific angle of sunlight on the water, the texture of her small hand when he had held her that morning before they left for the beach. When these memories surfaced unbidden—triggered by the sight of a child's small wrist, or by overhearing someone mention a family losing a son—the auditory details would flood back with excruciating clarity. He would hear, as though it were happening again, the exact pitch of his brother's voice calling his name, the hollow sound of the ocean. And with that sensory replay came a grief so overwhelming that it seemed to stop his breathing.

Marcus had come to believe, in the years that followed, that he was fundamentally weak. A man who was truly capable, truly strong, would have been watching more carefully. He would have anticipated the danger. The fact that he had failed to protect Aroha proved something essential about his character—that beneath the competence he showed the families who employed him, beneath his reliability and his gentleness with children, he was hollow. He felt, increasingly, like an object moving through the world rather than a person inhabiting it. This belief had a peculiar effect on how he encountered reminders of his failure. When a child in his care mentioned losing a pet, or when he overheard talk of people grieving the death of a loved one, Marcus would feel the weight of his own weakness crystallize. These conversations became unbearable triggers not simply because they evoked the memory of Aroha, but because they confirmed what he now knew about himself: that he was incapable of protecting anyone, that his presence in a child's life was ultimately a liability. His conviction that he had failed to protect his daughter made it impossible to hear such talk without his mind immediately returning to the specific details of that afternoon—the sound of the water, the exact position of the sun—and with those details came the crushing knowledge of his inadequacy.

Over time, Marcus had developed an almost reflexive avoidance of situations involving water or children's bodies. He had stopped working for one family entirely when they mentioned planning a beach trip. He no longer attended family gatherings where his brother's other children were present; seeing them felt like a confrontation with the child he could not save. His remaining employers had begun to notice a change—a new hesitation around bath time, a reluctance to take the children to parks with pools nearby. One family had recently asked whether he was still comfortable with his role. Marcus was not certain he was. What terrified him most was not the memory itself, but the fear that his weakness would somehow reach out and harm another child in his care, that his failure with Aroha was not an isolated tragedy but evidence of something dangerous in him. He had come to the clinic because the isolation had become complete, and because he could no longer distinguish between protecting children from harm and protecting them from himself.
